title: Gaius, Diotrephes, and Demetrius
summary: The elder writes to his friend Gaius, rejoicing that he walks in the truth and praising his faithful hospitality to traveling Christian workers, even strangers. He contrasts Gaius with Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first, rejects the elder's authority, slanders him, and expels those who welcome the travelers. The elder urges Gaius to imitate what is good, commends Demetrius, and hopes to visit soon.
story: Third John is the companion of Second John. There the elder warned a church not to host teachers who denied Christ; here he rebukes a leader who refuses to host workers who serve Christ, and he thanks a friend who does. Together the two letters show a church learning discernment in its hospitality: neither open to everyone nor closed to everyone, but faithful to the truth. The letter gives an unusually personal glimpse of the churches of Asia at the end of the first century, with named individuals, a church conflict, and a letter-carrier.
historical:
Like the other letters of John, Third John is usually dated around AD 85 to 100 and placed in the region of Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia. The elder has authority over more than one congregation and sends out traveling workers, who report back to him. He has already written to the church where Diotrephes is prominent (verse 9), perhaps a letter now lost, though some have suggested it was Second John. Diotrephes refused to receive it.

We know nothing about Gaius, Diotrephes, or Demetrius beyond this letter. Gaius was an extremely common Roman name, and the New Testament mentions several people called Gaius (in Macedonia, Derbe, and Corinth); there is no evidence linking any of them to this one. Diotrephes, whose name means nourished by Zeus, is a Greek name. Scholars have read his conflict with the elder as personal ambition, as local church leadership resisting the authority of a traveling or senior leader, or as an early stage in the development of a single presiding bishop in each city. The letter itself describes his behavior, not his office or his motives beyond loving to be first.
cultural:
Travel in the Roman world was common but costly and risky. Inns had a poor reputation, and travelers depended on networks of family, friends, and patrons. Early Christians built such a network out of their churches. To send someone on their way (verse 6) meant providing food, money, and perhaps companions for the next stage of the trip, and it was a recognized Christian duty (see Romans 15:24 and Titus 3:13). The traveling workers accepted nothing from the Gentiles (verse 7), meaning they did not take support from unbelievers, which set them apart from the many wandering teachers and philosophers who lived on public gifts and were often suspected of preaching for profit.

The elder's opening wish, that Gaius may prosper in every way and enjoy good health, follows the standard form of ancient letters. Surviving papyrus letters from the period regularly open with a prayer or wish for the recipient's health. Letters of recommendation were also common, and verse 12 functions as one for Demetrius, who probably carried this letter.
literary: Third John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count, and it follows the ordinary form of a Greco-Roman personal letter more closely than any other New Testament writing: sender, recipient, health wish, expression of joy, body, and closing greetings. The body sets three men side by side. Gaius (verses 1-8) is praised; Diotrephes (verses 9-10) is rebuked; Demetrius (verse 12) is commended. Verse 11 stands between them as the moral: do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The word beloved addresses Gaius four times, and truth recurs as it does in Second John. The closing (verses 13-14) closely parallels the end of Second John.

outline.t: Greeting and joy at Gaius's walk in the truth
Diotrephes, who loves to be first
Hope of a visit and greetings

doctrines.note: The traveling workers went out for the sake of the Name, and those who support them become fellow workers for the truth (verse 8). Mission is shared by those who go and those who send.
The letter shows the church as a network of congregations linked by letters, visits, and hospitality, and it exposes the danger of leadership that treats a congregation as one's own domain.

The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God (verse 11). Holiness is shown in ordinary conduct, such as welcoming strangers, telling the truth about others, and refusing to seek first place.

words.note: Philoproteuo, to love to be first, found only here in the New Testament. It captures Diotrephes' fault in a single word: ambition for preeminence. It stands in sharp contrast to Jesus' teaching that whoever wants to be first must be last and servant of all (Mark 9:35).

Propempo, to send on one's way, to escort or supply a traveler for the next stage. In the New Testament it became almost a technical term for church support of missionaries. The elder asks Gaius to do it in a manner worthy of God.

Synergos, fellow worker, one who labors alongside another. Paul uses it often for his coworkers. The elder applies it to all who support traveling missionaries: by giving hospitality, Gaius shares in the work itself.

christ: Christ is present in this letter through the Name (verse 7), a way early Christians spoke of Jesus himself, for whose sake the workers went out. The letter shows what life under that Name looks like in practice: welcoming strangers, sharing resources, supporting those who spread the message, and refusing to use power for self-promotion. Diotrephes' love of being first is the opposite of the Christ who came not to be served but to serve. Gaius's hospitality reflects Jesus' teaching that whoever receives one he sends receives him (John 13:20).

hard.q: Does verse 2 promise that faithful Christians will prosper financially and enjoy good health?
hard.a:
The verse has often been used to support the teaching that God wills material wealth and physical health for every believer who has enough faith. Read in its setting, it does not carry that weight. The elder is following the ordinary convention of ancient letters, which commonly opened with a wish for the recipient's health and well-being, much as a modern letter might say I hope you are well. He expresses a friend's prayer for Gaius, not a promise to all Christians.

The verb translated prosper (euodoo) originally meant to have a good road and so to succeed or go well; it does not refer specifically to money. The New Testament elsewhere presents faithful believers who were poor, sick, and persecuted, and Jesus warned against the love of wealth. At the same time, the verse does show that it is right to pray for another's bodily health and ordinary welfare. God cares about the whole person, and the elder's prayer is warm and practical, even if it is not a guarantee.

questions: Gaius was praised for welcoming workers who were strangers to him. Who are the strangers in your church or community whose work you could support?
Diotrephes loved to be first. Where do you see that desire in church life, or in yourself, and what does it cost others?
The elder says his greatest joy is to hear that his children walk in the truth. Whose faithfulness brings you that kind of joy, and have you told them?
